video.title: This $15K/Person Grant Feels Like a Cheat Code

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hector, who built an online, grant-funded trade school in Texas (about $2.4M in year one) and now consults for people starting schools. The core idea is that US workforce grants (WIOA-style, called 'WA' in the transcript) pay $5k-$15k per student, so a school can white-label a course and have the government pay the tuition. Variants include embedding a school in an existing business that struggles to hire (e.g. CNAs), on-the-job-training wage subsidies, and a school plus staffing placement combo. The key takeaway is that the arbitrage is navigating grant bureaucracy and enrolling students, but it is heavily US-state-specific.

speakers.name: Hector
speakers.description: Texas-based former online trade school operator, now consultant helping people start grant-funded trade schools

ideas.name: Grant-funded online trade school (white-label courses)
ideas.one_liner: Start an online vocational school, white-label courses, and have state workforce grants pay $5k-$15k per student.
ideas.business_model: Tuition paid by government workforce grant per enrolled student; margin over white-labelled course cost.
ideas.customer: Laid-off workers, people on food stamps/benefits, warehouse, retail and fast-food workers, nonprofit and shelter clients who qualify for the grant.
ideas.problem: People qualify for free training grants but find the process bureaucratic and do not know about it; there is a shortage of tradespeople and technicians.
ideas.offer: Free training (plus free laptop or VR goggles) toward a certificate in a technician or remote-capable field, paid for by the state grant.

pricing.model: Grant pays per student, varying by state, region and field
pricing.notes: White-label course cost $800-$1,000 (later $500 example); equipment such as goggles $200-$300 or a laptop.

acquisition_channels.details: Pitched the grant to churches, church groups, women's shelters, nonprofits, workforce development centres and chambers of commerce as community/referral partners; spent $0 on marketing.

quote.text: I went I spent zero dollars in marketing. I just went knocking on church doors and getting involved with church groups
quote.speaker: Hector

acquisition_channels.details: Got on Twitter, which produced his first consulting call (a flight attendant school in Minnesota).

ideas.delivery: Online courses licensed from a white-label provider, delivered remotely; some students receive laptops or VR goggles. Hands-on trades like welding or phlebotomy need in-person components or employer externships.
unit_economics_claims: Grant pays $5k-$15k per student depending on region, state and field
White-label course costs $800-$1,000, rest is margin
Scaled to about $2.4M in year one on grants in Texas
ideas.startup_cost: Low: white-label course about $500-$1,000 plus $200-$300 goggles or a laptop per student; state licensing fees and waits not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Varies by state: easy states quick, tough states wait 6 months to 2 years for approval (Florida, California, New York, Washington).

acquisition.how: Relied on in-person church and community outreach; enrolment is sales-driven. Online ads or SEO could be added but the grant message needs trust-building.

onboarding.how: Grant paperwork, eligibility checks and student enrolment can be partly handled by forms and CRM but require human government liaison.

delivery.how: Pre-built white-label online courses are largely software-delivered; some hybrid hands-on components need humans.

billing.how: Reimbursement from state or workforce boards needs compliance documentation and human follow-up.

support.how: Student support and job placement help can be mostly agent-handled with human escalation.

uk_applicability.notes: Depends on US state/federal workforce grants; the UK has different funded-training systems (e.g. apprenticeship levy, Skills Bootcamps, Adult Education Budget) with approved-provider registers and Ofqual/OFS rules, so the model would need a full rebuild.

risks: State licensing delays (up to two years in some states)
Grant rules vary by region and can change
Hard to get trust from skeptical students ('what's the catch')
Some trades cannot be taught online

ideas.name: In-house school bolt-on for employers (train your own staff)
ideas.one_liner: Help businesses with staff shortages open a grant-funded school to get paid to train and certify their own employees.
ideas.business_model: Consulting/setup for employers; the employer earns grant revenue per trained employee and can sell trainees to others.
ideas.customer: Business owners struggling to hire technicians or certified staff (e.g. adult daycare, HVAC, garage door repair).
ideas.problem: Constant staff shortage and high recruiting costs; staff are often uncertified.
ideas.offer: Stand up a school attached to the existing business, get $7,500 per certified employee, and farm out surplus graduates.

pricing.model: Not stated for consulting; grant revenue is $7,500 per trained staff member in the example

acquisition_channels.details: Case study came via mutual connections; Hector invites business owners with staffing pain to talk.

ideas.delivery: Consultant sets up the school, compliance, curriculum (white-label) and sales systems; the employer trains staff.
unit_economics_claims: Adult daycare owner could make about $300k extra revenue
Removes recruiting spend of tens to hundreds of thousands per year

acquisition.how: Relies on relationships and calls; UK cold outreach to businesses is feasible but needs trust.

delivery.how: Setup requires regulatory expertise and human work.

uk_applicability.notes: US grant dependent; UK analogue would be becoming an approved apprenticeship/training provider.

risks: Employer may not want to be in the school business

quotes.text: he's going to get 7500s for every single staff member he certifies that he needs to certify anyway
quotes.speaker: Hector

ideas.name: On-the-job training wage subsidy broker
ideas.one_liner: Help employers claim workforce-office subsidies of up to 100% of trainee wages and place graduates with them.
ideas.business_model: Middleman fee for placing trainees with employers, possibly margin on subsidies (not stated).
ideas.customer: Small businesses such as HVAC firms needing technicians.
ideas.problem: Employers don't know free labour subsidies exist and the offer sounds like a scam.
ideas.offer: Register as a training provider, get up to 300 hours of subsidised labour at up to $20-$22 an hour with workers' comp.

pricing.notes: Subsidy up to 100% of wages (up to $20-22/hr), worst case 50%.

acquisition_channels.details: Hector cold called 10 HVAC companies; 7 left messages unreturned after a month, 3 mom-and-pop firms declined.

quote.text: out of the 10 company I called I left messages for Seven of them still haven't heard back.
quote.speaker: Hector

ideas.delivery: Matches trained graduates to employers and handles workforce-office registration.
unit_economics_claims: Up to 300 hours of subsidised labour
Local workforce office has about $1M a year for employers and struggles to spend it

acquisition.how: Cold calling proved low-yield and UK TPS rules apply; limited-company email is allowed but trust is the barrier.

uk_applicability.notes: US-specific programmes; UK has different wage-subsidy schemes.

quotes.text: It's 300 hours of free labor up to 22 bucks an hour with works comp.
quotes.speaker: Hector

ideas.name: Trade school consulting (enrolment, sales and grant optimisation)
ideas.one_liner: Consult for existing school owners on pricing, grant use, CRM, sales scripts, funnels and enrolment.
ideas.business_model: Consulting for school owners (fee not stated).
ideas.customer: Small trade/vocational school owners who are tradespeople, not marketers.
ideas.problem: Owners undercharge, avoid grants, lack CRM and sales process.
ideas.offer: Re-price using grants, bundle courses, add job placement, install sales training, scripting, email campaigns and funnels.

pricing.notes: Hector admitted he gave away the Georgia help free early on.

lessons.lesson: Government-funded demand removes customer payment friction; the real edge is simplifying a bureaucratic process others find too complicated.

quote.text: they make it extremely complicated and then I was able to simplify.
quote.speaker: Hector

lessons.lesson: Tradespeople-turned-school-owners often undercharge and skip grants; the opportunity is in sales, pricing and process, not the craft.
Turning a cost centre (recruiting) into a profit centre (paid training) is a powerful framing for employers.
Curiosity on a routine call (an insurance enquiry) led to discovering a whole industry.
Find the real blocker to adoption (students had no laptops) and fix it; adding a free laptop increased usage.
Online-only delivery lets a school market statewide rather than being limited to a local area.
Cold outreach to small employers about subsidies had very low response; 'too good to be true' offers need trust and warm intros.
Regulatory friction (slow state approval) is a moat for those willing to wait.

evidence_quality.rationale: Hector's own $2.4M year-one claim is first-hand but unverified and details of how the margin was earned are thin; most other figures are second-hand client claims or hypotheticals. The transcript is vague on the grant name, legal specifics and fees.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Hector consults on starting schools and invites business owners to contact him; Koerner promotes Go High Level and the TK Owners community.
